title: Short Stuff: Foie Gras
summary: Short Stuff episode on foie gras. Josh opens with banter about Jerry and a joke about a custom "Jerry brand" miso, then explains foie gras as fattened goose or duck liver, its French origin, and the controversy over gavage (force-feeding). Covers the history: an ancient Egyptian origin tied to migratory waterfowl, and a chef named Jean Joseph Klaus (also rendered Klaussa) credited with creating foie gras in 1779 and patenting it, with King Louis XVI giving him a reward. They discuss prices of $40 to $80 a pound, the New York foie gras ban passed in 2019 (bill S.7894 is the bill number they reference as "the seventy eight bill"), and bans in India, Australia, and California. Pro-foie gras arguments include chef defenses, a Serious Eats article, the Catskill Foie Gras Collective's unconstitutionality challenge, and the claim that ducks and geese have an esophagus that stretches and does not cause much discomfort. Josh notes abusive farms exist and that the chicken egg industry is arguably treated as badly. Chuck mentions his past work in the chicken farming industry as a marketing person. Closes with sign-off and a plug for iHeartRadio.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh opens the Short Stuff episode with joking banter about Jerry and a 'Jerry brand' miso idea, then introduces foie gras as a controversial food, noting that the name translates from French roughly to 'fatty liver'.

segments.title: Foie gras ban and gavage
segments.summary: The hosts describe foie gras as a controversial food, note Josh's personal dislike of organ meats, and cover New York's 2019 bill banning force-fed products, which mainly targets foie gras. They mention similar bans in India, Australia, and California and name the practice of force-feeding as gavage.

segments.title: History of foie gras
segments.summary: The hosts trace the practice back to ancient Egypt, where waterfowl naturally fattened their livers before migration and people began force-feeding them. The practice spread to the Mediterranean and France. Chef Jean Joseph Klaus is credited with creating foie gras in 1779 and patenting it, and King Louis XVI reportedly gave him a reward.

segments.title: How foie gras is made and its cost
segments.summary: The hosts explain that waterfowl naturally store fat in their livers, and that foie gras is a fattened liver that tastes different from pate. They note prices of roughly $40 to $80 a pound, driven by labor-intensive production and luxury accompaniments such as brandy and truffles.

segments.title: Animal welfare arguments against foie gras
segments.summary: The hosts outline the animal rights case: force feeding involves tubes, ducks can hyperventilate or bleed, and birds are shackled. They mention the 2019 bill penalties of $500 to $2,000 in New York.

segments.title: Defenses of foie gras and the Catskill challenge
segments.summary: The hosts describe chef defenses of foie gras, including a Serious Eats article arguing it is unfairly targeted. They cover the Catskill Foie Gras Collective's unconstitutionality challenge and its leader Marcus Henley's claim that the feeding tube does not cause discomfort to ducks.

segments.title: Anatomy argument and abusive farms
segments.summary: The hosts explain the argument that duck and goose esophaguses are separate from the trachea and can stretch, so force feeding causes little discomfort, and that liver enlargement is a natural process being simulated. They acknowledge that abusive farms exist with broken beaks and bleeding, and that good foie gras comes from humanely treated birds.

segments.title: Chicken egg industry comparison and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Josh says the strongest counterargument is that chicken egg production is treated just as badly. Chuck shares his past work as a marketing person in the chicken farming industry. The hosts close with personal reflections and a brief look at the unconstitutionality question.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh wraps up, encouraging listeners to research foie gras and make up their own minds, and gives the show credits and a plug for iHeartRadio.
